concept.name: Reverse Proxy Patterns & Edge Load Balancing
concept.tagline: Terminate TLS, pool upstream TCP sockets, balance traffic across fleets, and enforce rate limits using NGINX, HAProxy, and Envoy.

spark.summary: A reverse proxy acts as an intermediary gateway positioned between external clients and private backend services. It terminates client TLS handshakes, multiplexes requests across persistent upstream connection pools, distributes traffic via balancing algorithms (Round Robin, Least Connections, P2C), and guards internal services against direct internet exposure.
spark.keyTakeaway: Offload TLS decryption, header sanitation, and connection pooling to the reverse proxy tier (Envoy, NGINX) to prevent backend worker exhaustion; configure health-checked connection pools and active outlier detection to isolate failing upstream instances without cascading outages.

concept.whyItMatters: Exposing internal microservices directly to client networks forces every application instance to manage TLS certificates, handle slow client attacks (Slowloris), and execute complex routing. Placing an optimized reverse proxy layer at the edge decouples routing policy from application logic, slashes backend connection overhead by up to 90%, and provides centralized observability.
whenToUse: Microservice architectures needing unified entrypoints, TLS offloading, and path/header-based routing.
Shielding backend servers from slow clients, DDoS surges, and unauthorized direct IP access.
Canary deployments, blue-green traffic shifting, and shadow/mirror testing across software versions.
whenNotToUse: Simple monolithic applications deployed on single servers where an additional proxy hop adds latency without operational benefit.
Ultra-low latency HPC (High Performance Computing) or intra-node MPI workloads where sub-microsecond latency demands direct kernel bypass (e.g. DPDK, RDMA).
Direct peer-to-peer (P2P) mesh protocols where intermediaries break end-to-end direct UDP hole-punching.
keyPoints: TLS Termination & Offloading: Performs expensive asymmetric cryptography (RSA/ECDSA key exchange) once at the edge, forwarding plain HTTP/1.1 or gRPC over private, encrypted VPC networks.
Connection Multiplexing & Pooling: Converts thousands of slow, erratic client connections into a compact pool of warm, persistent HTTP/2 or TCP upstream connections.
Load Balancing Algorithms: Beyond Round-Robin, production proxies use Weighted Least Connections or Power of Two Choices (P2C) with Peak EWMA to avoid hot-spotting slower backend nodes.
Outlier Detection & Circuit Breaking: Automatically ejects backends returning 5xx spikes or high latency from the routing pool before cascading failures consume downstream services.
Header Manipulation & Security Enforcement: Strips untrusted external headers, injects tracing identifiers (x-request-id), and terminates hop-by-hop HTTP headers.

examples.title: Envoy Upstream Connection Pooling at Scale
examples.scenario: A backend payments cluster running on 20 nodes was overwhelmed by 40,000 incoming client TLS connections, spending 45% of its CPU on cryptographic handshakes.
examples.outcome: Deploying Envoy as an edge reverse proxy reduced backend TCP connections from 40,000 to 200 persistent pooled sockets, freeing 40% CPU capacity.

examples.title: Canary Shifting with Header-Based Routing
examples.scenario: An engineering team needed to test a new version of their recommendations engine against 5% of production traffic without deploying a separate domain.
examples.outcome: Configured reverse proxy weighted cluster matching to route 95% to v1 and 5% to v2, shifting to 100% automatically after error budget criteria were met.

tradeOffs.factor: Centralized Control vs Extra Network Hop
tradeOffs.pro: Centralizes TLS certs, rate-limiting rules, auth token validation, and distributed tracing headers in one layer.
tradeOffs.con: Adds an additional 0.5ms–2ms network latency hop and creates an edge infrastructure tier requiring dedicated operational ownership.

tradeOffs.factor: Connection Pooling vs Stale Upstream Sockets
tradeOffs.pro: Dramatically reduces backend handshake CPU costs and avoids slow-start latency.
tradeOffs.con: If upstreams restart without graceful shutdown, proxy connection pools can route requests to closed sockets unless TCP keepalives and active retries are configured.

tradeOffs.pro: Buffering request/response bodies shields backend workers from slow-upload clients (Slowloris mitigation).
tradeOffs.con: Increases proxy memory consumption and prevents low-latency real-time chunked streaming unless buffering is disabled explicitly.

failureModes.name: Upstream Thundering Herd & Blackholing
failureModes.description: When an upstream service restarts, the reverse proxy floods the cold nodes with thousands of simultaneous new connections, instantly crashing them before they can warm caches.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure slow-start warm-up ramps in Envoy/NGINX, enforce concurrency limits, and use health checks to stage node reintroduction.

failureModes.name: Buffer Exhaustion & Disk Spooling
failureModes.description: Clients uploading large payloads or backends returning large responses exceed proxy RAM buffers (client_body_buffer_size), causing the proxy to write chunks to disk and throttling throughput.
failureModes.mitigation: Stream large payloads directly without buffering, set strict max payload boundaries, and provision proxy nodes with fast NVMe swap or high RAM ceilings.

failureModes.name: Misconfigured X-Forwarded-For Trust
failureModes.description: Proxy fails to sanitize untrusted client X-Forwarded-For headers, allowing attackers to spoof client IP addresses and bypass IP-based rate limiters and geofences.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure real_ip_recursive or Envoy xff_num_trusted_hops to strip client-supplied headers and only trust the nearest legitimate network hop.

commonMistakes: Disabling upstream connection keepalives, forcing the proxy to perform a brand-new TCP handshake for every client request.
Omitting connect, read, and write timeouts, causing hung backend threads to consume proxy file descriptors until exhaustion.
Using pure Round-Robin on heterogeneous hardware or services with high variance in request execution times, leading to severe tail latency spikes.

caseStudy.problem: Managing edge traffic across hundreds of microservices required dynamic routing, canary deployments, and resilient retries without redeploying monolithic edge configurations.
caseStudy.solution: Developed Zuul 2 and later migrated to Envoy proxy fleets, implementing non-blocking Netty/epoll I/O filters, active outlier detection, and dynamic service discovery via Eureka and control plane APIs.
caseStudy.impact: Handled tens of millions of concurrent video streaming client sessions with sub-millisecond proxy overhead and automated failover across AWS availability zones.

relationships.description: Reverse proxies manage upstream and downstream TCP socket buffers, connections, and keepalive pools.
Reverse proxies can cache static or micro-cached HTTP responses in shared memory to shield backend clusters.
CDNs act as globally distributed reverse proxies terminating traffic close to users via Anycast routing.

questions.title: Upstream Keepalive Connection Pooling
questions.prompt: Why is configuring 'proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection "";' critical when configuring an NGINX reverse proxy to route to backend clusters?

options.text: By default, NGINX uses HTTP/1.0 with 'Connection: close' for upstreams; clearing the header and using HTTP/1.1 allows persistent socket reuse from the upstream keepalive pool.
options.explanation: Correct! Without these directives, NGINX closes the backend TCP socket after every single request, causing high CPU consumption from repeated handshakes and ephemeral port exhaustion.

options.text: It encrypts the payload using AES-256 before transmitting over the internal network.
options.explanation: HTTP version and Connection headers do not handle symmetric payload encryption.

options.text: It disables all HTTP caching on the proxy.
options.explanation: Upstream connection headers regulate transport socket reuse, not caching headers like Cache-Control.

options.text: It bypasses the proxy event loop and streams directly to disk.
options.explanation: It enables socket reuse within the event loop.

rubric.excellent: Identifies default HTTP/1.0 behavior and explains how keepalive connection pools eliminate handshake overhead.
rubric.gap: Confuses connection headers with encryption or caching.

questions.sampleSolution: By default, NGINX forwards requests using HTTP/1.0 with Connection: close, destroying the TCP socket; clearing the header enables persistent keepalive pool reuse.
questions.explanation: Always enable HTTP/1.1 and clear the Connection header for upstreams in NGINX.

interviewProblems.title: Designing a Multi-Tenant Edge Gateway Tier
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design an edge reverse proxy tier handling 50,000 requests per second across 50 distinct microservices. How do you handle routing, TLS termination, backend health checking, and prevent noisy neighbors from crashing the tier?
constraints: Must isolate slow backend services from consuming all proxy worker threads
Must support automated canary deployments with weighted traffic shifting
Must achieve sub-3ms p99 proxy overhead

dimensions.name: Resilience & Isolation
dimensions.description: Implements circuit breakers, outlier detection, and per-service connection pools.

dimensions.name: Traffic Management
dimensions.description: Configures weighted routing, header matching, and TLS termination.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Use Envoy proxy with P2C load balancing, configure isolated connection pools and circuit breakers per upstream cluster, terminate TLS at the edge with session tickets, and enforce token bucket rate limits per tenant.
commonPitfalls: Sharing a global unbounded connection pool across all microservices.
